card.name: Phathisi
card.tagline: Bakwena leg-rattle dance with pegged, short trousers
card.profile: Phathisi is a traditional dance of the Bakwena tribe of Botswana, characterized by men dancing with the lower legs of the trousers tied off with a peg (or short animal-skin pants called tshega) and by vigorous, fast footwork with leg rattles (KnowBotswana; Setapa/Wikipedia). It is one of the principal Tswana dance styles alongside setapa and borankana, performed to a lead singer and chorus with handclaps, foot-stamping and ankle rattles in a brisk compound meter.
card.insight: Phathisi's distinctive pegged-trouser style was influential enough to be borrowed by neighboring traditions — the Bangwaketse incorporated it as "Setapa sa phathisi" — showing how Tswana dance forms circulated and blended across tribal boundaries in Botswana (Setapa, Wikipedia).

card.profile_long: Phathisi, also alternatively referred to as Borankana, is a traditional music and dance tradition deeply connected to the culture of Botswana, specifically practiced and performed by the Bakwena tribe residing in the Kweneng District, with its center in Molepolole. Historically, performances of Borankana are estimated to have initiated between the years 1914 and 1916. According to historical accounts, the tradition of Phathisi emerged from a very specific utilitarian necessity: men tying down the lowest part of their trousers using a peg when cycling. During this historical era, men frequently worked in mines and relied on bicycles for transportation. Owning a bicycle was a sign of relative wealth, requiring riders to tightly secure their trouser legs to prevent them from being caught in the bicycle chain or causing the rider to topple over. This practical method of trouser pegging was subsequently adapted into the performance style of Borankana, before eventually shifting from pegged trousers to the use of shorts during performances. Traditionally, Borankana was performed exclusively during tribal activities, serving as a vital cultural expression for the community. The performance structure involves distinct gender roles: men and boys are the ones who do the dancing, while females participate actively by singing, clapping hands, and ululating throughout the performance. Both elderly people and young people of the Bakwena tribe participate in keeping this traditional music and dance alive. The dance form bridges daily working-class life—specifically the bicycle commutes of mine workers—with cultural heritage in the Kweneng District. While specific technical descriptions of footwork, posture, musical instruments, and spatial formations are not detailed in the sources, the historical narrative surrounding Phathisi provides a clear window into how practical innovations in daily dress transformed into enduring cultural performance arts within Botswana.

observation.setting: open-air dirt ground arena with bleachers and spectators surrounding the perimeter under shaded canopies
observation.dancers: a large group of male and female dancers in traditional attire
observation.formation_and_space: group arranged initially in a line, moving in unison, forming a tight multi-row formation, and some solo dancers moving around the main group
observation.posture: torsos leaning forward slightly with bent knees and weight kept low
observation.footwork: stamping, hopping, and high knee lifts on the beat, creating dust
observation.arms_and_hands: arms held up or extending outwards, holding wooden poles across shoulders or whips
observation.hips_and_torso: bouncing and undulating torso matching the leg movements
observation.levels_jumps_turns: frequent lowering into deep knee bends and drops to the ground, rising with high stamps and jumps
observation.costume_and_props: matching brown animal hide skirts or shorts, patterned shin guards or leg wraps, bare chests, and wooden poles carried on shoulders
observation.cannot_infer: exact footwork details obscured by dust kicked up from the dirt floor and low resolution of the video

signature_moments.what: dancers holding poles across their shoulders drop synchronously to their knees on the dirt ground
dancers fall smoothly to the ground and slide or crawl forward in unison while keeping upper bodies low
dancers raise both arms overhead while executing rapid, high knee lifts and stamping in place
